mcqs.question: A load balancer marks a server unhealthy after noticing the last 5 real user requests to it all timed out, without sending any extra probe traffic. Which type of health check is this?
options: An active health check, because it actively removes the server
A passive health check, because it infers health from real traffic outcomes instead of sending its own probes
A synthetic health check, because it simulates a fake user
A weighted health check, because it weighs multiple servers against each other
mcqs.explanation: Passive checks are defined by watching real traffic outcomes rather than sending independent probes — 'active' names the opposite kind of check (proactive probing), and removal is a consequence, not the check type. 'Synthetic' and 'weighted' aren't standard names for either check type described here.

mcqs.question: A team sets their health check to fail after just 1 missed check, polled every 2 seconds. Under mild network jitter, what is the most likely outcome?
options: Faster, more accurate detection of genuine node failures with no downside
The node will never be marked unhealthy under any circumstances
Flapping — the node repeatedly bounces in and out of rotation on transient blips that aren't real failures
The load balancer will automatically increase the threshold on its own to compensate
mcqs.explanation: A 1-failure threshold reacts to a single dropped health-check packet as if it were a real outage — exactly the flapping failure mode from the trade-off. It isn't accuracy without downside (that ignores the false-positive cost), it doesn't mean the node is never marked unhealthy, and load balancers don't self-tune thresholds.

mcqs.question: A node dies abruptly (not gracefully drained) while it has in-flight requests. What happens to those specific in-flight requests?
options: The load balancer automatically completes them using a cached copy of the request
They are silently retried by the load balancer an unlimited number of times until they succeed
They are queued indefinitely until the node comes back online
They fail outright, and it's up to the client or an upstream retry policy to resend them to a different, healthy node
mcqs.explanation: A load balancer has no way to resume or replay a request whose backend disappeared mid-processing — it isn't caching responses, retrying automatically without a configured policy, or queuing indefinitely. The failure surfaces to the caller, which is exactly why idempotent request design and a real retry policy matter upstream of the load balancer.

mcqs.question: An app server's `/health` endpoint returns 200 OK by simply checking that the HTTP server process is running, with no other logic. The app's database connection pool is actually exhausted and every real request is failing. What does the health check miss?
options: It only checks that the process is alive, not that the dependencies (like the database connection) the app actually needs are working — so it can't detect 'alive but useless'
Nothing — a 200 OK from any endpoint is sufficient proof the app is fully healthy
The health check is checking the wrong HTTP status code entirely
The load balancer should be using a passive check instead, which would have caught this automatically without any code changes
mcqs.explanation: This is the shallow-check trap directly: responding at all isn't the same as being able to serve real requests. Treating any 200 OK as proof of full health is the wrong belief this pitfall warns against. The status code isn't the issue — the endpoint's logic is. And a passive check would eventually catch it via failed real requests, but that means real users hit the failure first — it's a backstop, not a substitute for a deeper active check.

mcqs.question: Why do production load balancers typically require fewer consecutive successes to mark a node unhealthy than to mark it healthy again?
options: It's arbitrary and has no operational reasoning behind it
Removing a bad node quickly limits blast radius, while re-adding one slowly protects against a node that's still flaky or warming up right after recovering
Health checks can only run in one direction, so the asymmetry is a technical limitation
Marking a node healthy again is always instantaneous and needs no threshold at all
mcqs.explanation: The asymmetry is a deliberate design choice: fast removal caps damage from a bad node, while slow re-addition avoids trusting a node that might still be intermittently broken. It isn't arbitrary, isn't a technical limitation of the check direction, and re-addition does use its own threshold, just a stricter one.

mcqs.question: Several nodes recover from an outage and pass health checks at nearly the same time, then immediately fail again under full production traffic. What's the most likely cause?
options: The health checks themselves were misconfigured with too long an interval
All the nodes were re-admitted to full traffic at once with cold caches and connection pools, and the sudden load re-failed them; gradual re-admission (slow start) is the standard fix
This can only be caused by a bug in the load balancer's routing algorithm
The nodes were never actually healthy, and the health check was a false positive
mcqs.explanation: This is the thundering-herd-on-recovery failure mode: passing a health check only proves the node responds, not that it can absorb full traffic cold, and dumping 100% of traffic on newly-healthy nodes at once can re-fail them. It's not a check-interval issue, not necessarily a routing bug, and the check wasn't a false positive — the node was genuinely healthy, just not warmed up.
